title: Compassion for the one who harms
hookLine: the manuals: feel compassion even for a wrongdoer, who is heading toward suffering

cards: Compassion for the sick is easy to understand. For the grieving, the lost, the frightened: of course. But what about the person who cheated, lied, hurt someone you love?
When they finally get what's coming, the feeling can be closer to satisfaction. The old Buddhist manual goes somewhere that can feel almost backward at first.
The one doing harm, it says, is someone to feel compassion for too. Not because harm doesn't matter. Because of where it leads.

teach.b: The Visuddhimagga gives a picture. A thief has been caught, and is being led through the streets to his execution. People who see him feel a pang, the manual says: that poor man is walking to his death.
Now look at anyone who does harm the same way.

Even if they're laughing now, rich and comfortable, they are walking toward suffering, because in Buddhist teaching, harmful actions ripen into pain for the one who does them. So this compassion isn't approval.
It's seeing where the road goes. A story in the suttas shows what this looks like in person.

In the Buddha's time, a man called Angulimala was terrorizing a region of Kosala, killing people and, the story says, wearing a garland of their fingers. People along the road warned the Buddha not to go on.
He walked it anyway. Angulimala chased him, running as hard as he could, and couldn't catch up with the Buddha, who was only walking. He shouted, stop!
And the Buddha said: I have stopped, Angulimala. You stop too. Those words broke something open.
Angulimala threw away his weapons and became a monk. The story doesn't say his actions vanished; people still threw stones at him on his alms rounds, and the Buddha told him to bear it.
Compassion doesn't cancel consequences, and it doesn't mean staying near someone dangerous.
It means that, from a safe distance, you can still see a person walking toward pain, and wish them a different road.

how: Buddhist teachers encourage extending compassion even to people who do harm, starting with small cases, while being clear that this doesn't excuse harm or require staying near danger; the Angulimala story is widely told, and a verse linked to him is chanted for safe childbirth in Theravada communities.

o: a king of Kosala who protected the early monks
a killer who became a monk after meeting the Buddha
a forest hermit who taught the Buddha meditation

games.q: match each piece of today's teaching.
p: a killer who became a monk

s: compassion for the one who harms means approving of the harm
it means seeing where their road leads; it isn't approval.
in the story, Angulimala couldn't catch the Buddha, who was only walking
then the Buddha said: I have stopped; you stop too.
the manuals suggest starting with the worst person you know
they suggest starting small and working outward.

games.q: you're the Buddha. people along the way warn you not to take the road where the killer Angulimala waits. what do you do?
games.why: he walked it. Angulimala couldn't catch him, shouted stop, and heard: I have stopped; you stop too. he threw away his weapons and became a monk.

practice: Bring to mind someone who has done a small harm, not the worst person you know, and not someone who hurt you deeply; the manuals say to start small.
See the road they're on, where behavior like that usually leads, loneliness, fear, more trouble, and let the heart tremble a little for where they're heading.
If you can, offer one breath of the wish, may you find a different road, and then let them go.

wordCard.voice: Angulimala. The killer turned monk whom the Buddha didn't flee, telling him simply: I have stopped, you stop too.

orig.note: Pali Aṅgulimāla, a name meaning 'finger garland': aṅguli (finger) and mālā (garland).

carryVoice: Your line: they are heading for pain. Not approval: a wish for a different road. Two hundred thirty-seven days, and counting.

sources.ref: Visuddhimagga IX (compassion for an evil-doer: the robber led to execution)
